runs.text: A recursive subprogram solves a problem by asking itself for a smaller version, until it reaches one it already knows how to solve.
The problem
The tower of Hanoi:
three discs
of different sizes are stacked on post
A
, from the biggest at the bottom to the smallest at the top. They have to go to post
C
, moving
one disc at a time
and never putting a big disc on a small one. Post
B
helps.
Which moves do you have to make, and how many are there?
Try it
Solve it with three coins of different sizes on three pieces of paper marked A, B and C.
There are
moves: small from A to C, middle from A to B, small from C to B, big from A to C, small from B to A, middle from B to C and small from A to C.
Understand and plan

entries.text: What goes in and what comes out?
The number of discs goes in; the moves come out, in order.
Itself. To move 3 discs from A to C you first have to move the top 2 to B, and that is the same problem with one disc less.
Which parts does it split into?
It splits into three: move 2 discs from A to B, move the big one from A to C and move the 2 from B to C. Moving a single disc is direct.

runs.text: The small disc goes from A to C.
The middle one goes from A to B.
The small one goes from C to B: the tower of two is on B.
The big one goes from A to C.
The small one goes from B to A.
The middle one goes from B to C.
The small one goes from A to C: the whole tower is on C.
The new tool
A subprogram that calls itself uses
recursion
. It has two parts: the
base case
, solved without calling itself, and the
recursive case
, which calls itself with a smaller problem and has to get closer to the base case.

The next one is opened: another smaller one.
The smallest does not open: it is the base case.
They close from the inside out, with the result.

runs.text: The base case is a tower of 0 discs: there is nothing to move. The recursive case moves a tower of
discs, which gets closer to the base case with each call.
Test
With 1 disc there is a single move; with 0, none: it is the edge case the base case solves. Counting moves:
Each extra disc doubles the moves and adds one.
Improve
In one sentence:
To move a tower, the top tower is moved out of the way, the big disc is moved and the top tower is put back on top

The cost grows fast: with 20 discs there are more than a million moves. Recursion is not always the best option: the factorial does not branch, and a loop solves it just as clearly without opening a frame for each number.
What you learned

points.text: A recursive subprogram calls itself with a smaller problem.
The base case is solved without calling itself; the recursive case has to get closer to it.

runs.text: Practise

entries.text: The program calls itself endlessly until the engine stops it by depth. The find-the-error exercise shows it.
A recursive case that does not shrink.
Say, at each call, which number gets closer to zero.
Hanoi needs it; the factorial does not. Compare both versions.
